title: Mastery Challenge: Computers & the Internet
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Computers & the Internet Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: One question per chapter: gates, transistors, binary search, NAT, compression, password hashes, re-identification, feedback loops, chatbots and quantum. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Computers & the Internet Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from a single bit to judging a claim about AI. Level 1 followed one photo through the machine; now see how far you've come. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Computers & the Internet: mastered
learned: How bits, gates and a processor do all the work, and how that machine grew from punched cards to smartphones.
How software is translated and scheduled, and why some algorithms scale while others don't.
How addresses, DNS, routers and TCP carry a web page to your screen, and what makes it slow.
Why hashes, second factors and public keys protect you, and where your personal data really goes.
How algorithms and AI learn from data and where they fail, and which questions sort any tech claim.

questions.prompt: A porch light should turn on if motion is sensed or the manual switch is on. Which gate does that job?

options.label: OR
AND
options.rationale: AND would need both at once.

options.label: NOT
options.rationale: NOT flips one input.

options.label: No single gate
options.rationale: A single OR gate does it.

questions.explanation: OR outputs 1 when any input is 1, like two switches wired in parallel.

questions.prompt: Why did the transistor take over from the vacuum tube as the computer's switch?

options.label: It could hold many states at once, not just on and off
options.rationale: It's still an on-off switch, like the tube.

options.label: It was the first switch able to store a bit at all
options.rationale: ENIAC's tubes were already switching bits.

options.label: It let computers change jobs without any rewiring
options.rationale: That was the stored program, a separate idea.

options.label: It was small, ran cool, used little power and rarely failed

questions.explanation: A tube had to heat its cathode to about 1,000°C and burned out; a transistor is small, cool, reliable and frugal.

questions.prompt: Binary search needs at most about 20 steps for a sorted list of a million names. About how many for 4 million?

options.rationale: That's two million; four million is one more doubling.
Doubling the list adds a step; it doesn't double the steps.
Four times the steps is how a linear search grows.

questions.explanation: Each doubling adds one question: 1 million takes about 20, 2 million about 21, 4 million about 22.

questions.prompt: Why can't a computer out on the internet start a conversation with your laptop at home, unless the router is set up for it?

options.label: Home laptops have no IP address of any kind on a home network
options.rationale: It has a private address, just not a public one.

options.label: DNS refuses to look up the names of devices inside people's homes
options.rationale: DNS turns names into addresses; it doesn't block packets.

options.label: The router's NAT table only lists conversations started from inside
Routers throw away every single packet that arrives from outside
options.rationale: Replies to your own requests come in fine.

questions.explanation: NAT writes each outgoing conversation into a table; an unasked packet from outside finds no entry to match.

questions.prompt: Lossy compression throws some detail away for good. Which file is it safe to use on?

options.label: A spreadsheet of your bank balances
options.rationale: Every digit has to come back exactly.

options.label: A holiday photo you're sharing online
A contract saved as a text document
options.rationale: Every character has to come back exactly.

options.label: A program's machine code instructions
options.rationale: One wrong byte changes what the processor does.

questions.explanation: Small errors spread over a picture are hard to see; in text or numbers, they change the meaning.

questions.prompt: A thief copies a well-run site's password list. Why can't they simply read the passwords?

options.label: The passwords are encrypted, and the key is hidden well
options.rationale: Hashing has no key; encryption would be riskier.

options.label: The list is stored in binary, which people can't read
options.rationale: Binary is just encoding; it hides nothing.

options.label: The site deletes the whole list after every login
options.rationale: The site keeps it to check each login.

options.label: The site kept only one-way hashes, never the passwords

questions.explanation: A hash can't be turned back into the password, so the site checks logins by hashing what you type and comparing.

questions.prompt: A study shares fitness records with names removed but keeps ZIP code, birth date and sex. Why is that risky?

options.label: Removing names makes any dataset fully anonymous
options.rationale: Names are only one way to point at a person.

options.label: ZIP codes are secret, so nobody else could match them
options.rationale: Voter lists carry them, along with names.

options.label: Together those details often match just one person
Fitness data can never be linked to another dataset
options.rationale: Linking to a voter list is exactly how it's done.

questions.explanation: A few details multiply into more combinations than people, so a list with names can put a name back on the record.

questions.prompt: A video app learns from what you click, but it also chose what you were shown. Why does that muddy its lesson?

options.label: It can't easily tell liking something from being shown it
It forgets every click the moment you close the app
options.rationale: Your clicks become its next lesson.

options.label: Clicks are metadata, so they can't be counted at all
options.rationale: Clicks are exactly what it counts.

options.label: It only learns from star ratings, never from clicks
options.rationale: Clicks are its main training data.

questions.explanation: The recommender trains on reactions it helped cause, so it can end up shaping the very data it learns from.

questions.prompt: Level 7's adder always gets 1 + 1 right. Why can a chatbot state a false fact as confidently as a true one?

options.label: It looks answers up in a database that contains errors
options.rationale: It generates text token by token, not by lookup.

options.label: It knows the answer is wrong but is built to hide it
options.rationale: It has no built-in check for truth, hidden or not.

options.label: It picks likely next tokens, and likely isn't true
Its adder circuits slip up on long, difficult sums
options.rationale: Adders follow fixed rules; next-token picks don't.

questions.explanation: An adder follows fixed rules; a language model follows statistical patterns, which reward fitting text, not truth.

questions.prompt: RSA's padlock from Level 55 rests on how hard it is to find two huge primes from their product. What would a large quantum computer mean for it?

options.label: Nothing, since no machine could ever factor such numbers
options.rationale: Shor's 1994 algorithm shows a large quantum computer could.

options.label: It could break it, so NIST has published post-quantum standards
It would break every kind of encryption and hashing at once
options.rationale: The threat is to public-key methods like RSA, not everything.

options.label: It would make RSA stronger, since qubits add extra security
options.rationale: Shor's algorithm points the other way.

questions.explanation: A large quantum computer would break RSA and elliptic-curve methods; NIST released its first post-quantum standards in 2024.
